n: Book Two of the Psalms begins here. The writer, from the temple singers called the sons of Korah, longs for God the way a thirsty deer longs for flowing streams in a dry land.

f.g: Stream beds that run with water — precious in a dry country.

n: His thirst is not for religion in general but for the living God himself. He aches to come again into God’s presence at the sanctuary.
He has cried so much that tears have been his only food. Meanwhile scoffers keep taunting, “So where is your God?”

f.g: In KJV English, “meat” means food in general.

n: He remembers happier days leading joyful crowds to the temple at festival time. The memory both comforts and hurts.

f.g: Celebrated a sacred festival, such as Passover or Tabernacles.

n: A refrain repeated in verse 11 and in Psalm 43: the psalmist speaks to his own soul, challenging despair with hope. This is a model of honest self-encouragement.

f.g: The saving help of his presence (literally, his face).

n: Far from Jerusalem, in the north near the Jordan’s headwaters and Mount Hermon, he chooses to remember God from where he is.

f.g: The peaks of Mount Hermon, at Israel’s northern border.
“Little mountain” — an unknown peak, perhaps near Hermon.

n: The roaring waterfalls of the north become a picture of his distress: wave upon wave of trouble crashing over him. Jonah later used this same language from inside the fish.

f.g: One roaring depth answers another — overwhelming, endless waters.

f.w: all thy waves and thy billows are gone over me

n: Yet even in this flood, God’s loyal love will come by day and his song will fill the night. Faith holds onto God through both light and dark.

f.w: in the night his song shall be with me

n: He brings his honest question to God, his rock: why have you forgotten me? The Psalms show that faithful people can ask hard questions.
The enemies’ daily taunt cuts like a sword into his bones.
The refrain returns, now calling God “the health of my countenance” — the one who will bring the light back to his face. Hope has the last word.

f.g: The salvation of my face — the one who will make me look up again.
